course.title: Linux Forensics
course.description: A Linux-specific practical forensics course covering evidence thinking, integrity and provenance, storage/VFS, ext4, timestamps, journald, Linux Audit, authentication, process and /proc triage, shell history, systemd and cron persistence, users and permissions, capabilities, xattrs and links, network/SSH evidence, package provenance, SQLite artifacts, current Volatility 3 Linux memory analysis, timelines, anti-forensics awareness, validation, reporting, and a read-only final triage workbench.
prerequisites: Basic Python is helpful for the final project
learningOutcomes: Map investigative questions to Linux evidence sources.
Preserve evidence integrity with hashes and provenance.
Interpret VFS, ext4, inode, journal, link, and timestamp concepts.
Query and interpret journald and Linux Audit records with retention limits.
Correlate authentication, process, service, persistence, permission, and network evidence.
Use /proc and current Volatility 3 Linux plugins for controlled triage.
Interpret package and SQLite application evidence.
Construct source-preserving timelines and evaluate alternative explanations.
Recognize evidence gaps and anti-forensics indicators cautiously.
Validate tools and write evidence-grounded findings.
Complete the read-only final triage workbench.

modules.title: Foundations, Scope, and Evidence Thinking
modules.description: Linux forensic foundations, investigative questions, evidence classes, integrity, and provenance.

lessons.title: Linux Evidence Landscape
lessons.description: Map Linux evidence across persistent storage, virtual kernel interfaces, logs, accounts, applications, network state, and memory.

notes.text: Linux evidence is distributed. Filesystem metadata, journals, audit records, shell histories, application data, network state, and RAM answer different questions.

items: Persistent evidence includes files, metadata, logs, configuration, and package data.
Volatile evidence includes processes, sockets, mounts, /proc state, and RAM.

quiz.question: Which source is inherently volatile?
options: It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: RAM and current process state
quiz.explanation: Processes and RAM change continuously; preserved copies do not have that same volatility.

summary: Linux forensic evidence is distributed across layers.
Artifact semantics matter as much as artifact presence.

lessons.title: Forensic Workflow
lessons.description: Follow preparation, preservation, acquisition, examination, analysis, reporting, and closure.

notes.text: NIST SP 800-86 frames forensics as a process involving files, operating systems, network traffic, and applications. It is guidance rather than legal advice or a universal investigation procedure.

items: Question-driven collection is preferable to indiscriminate collection.
Live acquisition may alter the source system.

quiz.question: What should drive evidence collection?
options: The investigative question and preservation requirements
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: The investigative question and preservation requirements
quiz.explanation: Collection should be justified by the question and the effect of the method on evidence.

summary: A defensible workflow is deliberate and documented.

lessons.title: Hashing and Provenance
lessons.description: Use hashes and evidence identifiers to protect integrity and preserve traceability.

notes.text: A SHA-256 digest is useful for detecting changes to represented bytes. It does not prove authorship, intent, or truthfulness.

items: Record case/evidence IDs, acquisition details, tool/version, and hashes.
Keep preserved evidence separate from working copies.

practicals.title: Verify a Working Copy
practicals.description: Hash a controlled lab file before and after copying, then modify only the working copy.
steps: Copy it to a separate directory.
Modify only the copy and hash again.
practicals.solution:
```bash
printf "forensic-lab\n" > source.txt
sha256sum source.txt
cp --preserve=all source.txt working.txt
sha256sum working.txt
printf "changed\n" >> working.txt
sha256sum working.txt
```
practicals.output: The source and unchanged copy should initially have the same digest; after modification the working-copy digest changes.

quiz.question: What does a SHA-256 comparison primarily establish?
options: It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: Whether represented bytes match
quiz.explanation: A hash comparison is an integrity/comparison operation.

summary: Integrity supports reproducibility but does not answer attribution questions.

tasks.title: Build a Linux Evidence Question Matrix
tasks.description: Map five investigation questions to Linux evidence sources.
tasks.problemStatement: A server may have experienced unauthorized administrative access. Build a matrix for authentication, execution, persistence, file activity, and time.
tasks.hint: Keep every proposed conclusion tied to a source artifact.
tasks.solutionCode: Example mapping: authentication→journald/audit; execution→audit/process; persistence→systemd/cron; file activity→filesystem metadata; time→multiple sources.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The matrix demonstrates question-driven collection and explicit limitations.

modules.title: Storage, VFS, ext4, and Timestamps
modules.description: Understand Linux storage layers and filesystem metadata needed for forensic interpretation.

lessons.title: Storage Layers and VFS
lessons.description: Distinguish block devices, partitions, filesystems, directories, and inodes.

notes.text: A disk or image can contain partitions and filesystems. The VFS gives userspace a common interface over different filesystem implementations.

items: A pathname is a namespace view, not a physical address.
Incorrect layer identification can invalidate higher-level parsing.

quiz.question: Why establish filesystem boundaries before parsing?
options: The parser needs the correct filesystem structures and offsets
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: The parser needs the correct filesystem structures and offsets
quiz.explanation: Forensic parsing depends on correct layer identification.

summary: Storage-layer understanding prevents false interpretations.

lessons.title: ext4 Inodes and Directory Entries
lessons.description: Understand inode metadata and how directory names map to inodes.
learningObjectives: distinguish directory entries from inode data

notes.text: ext4 inodes store metadata for filesystem objects. Directory entries associate names with inode numbers; a hard link can provide another name for the same inode.

items: Ownership, mode, size, and timestamps are metadata.
A pathname does not uniquely define filesystem object identity.

quiz.question: What is the relationship between a hard-linked name and an inode?
options: They can be two names for the same inode
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: They can be two names for the same inode
quiz.explanation: Hard links create multiple directory entries referring to the same inode.

summary: Filesystem identity is richer than a pathname.

lessons.title: ext4 Journaling
lessons.description: Explain journal purpose and forensic limitations.
learningObjectives: distinguish metadata journaling from activity logging

notes.text: Kernel documentation describes ext4 journaling as part of crash consistency. Under the usual data=ordered mode, metadata is journaled; the journal is not a complete user activity log.

items: Journal contents are finite and can be overwritten.
Use journal evidence with inode, log, and application evidence.

quiz.question: What is the safest description of the ext4 journal?
options: A filesystem-consistency mechanism that records journaled transactions
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: A filesystem-consistency mechanism that records journaled transactions
quiz.explanation: The journal supports filesystem consistency and recovery; it is not a universal history of user actions.

summary: Journal evidence must stay within documented ext4 semantics.

lessons.title: Linux Timestamps
lessons.description: Interpret atime, mtime, ctime, and optional birth-time fields without renaming their meaning.

notes.text: Linux atime concerns access, mtime concerns content modification, and ctime concerns inode/status change. ctime is not a generic creation timestamp.

items: Filesystem and kernel support determines whether birth time is available.
Preserve original timestamps and document any conversion.

practicals.title: Timestamp Lab
practicals.description: Observe how content and metadata changes affect stat output.
steps: Modify its contents and run stat.
practicals.solution:
```bash
printf "one\n" > sample.txt
stat sample.txt
printf "two\n" >> sample.txt
stat sample.txt
chmod 640 sample.txt
stat sample.txt
```
practicals.output: Exact timestamps vary. The expected learning result is correct interpretation of content and inode changes.

quiz.question: What does Linux ctime represent?
options: It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: The last inode/status change
quiz.explanation: Linux ctime represents inode/status change time rather than a generic creation timestamp.

summary: Timestamp semantics are platform-specific.

tasks.title: Classify Filesystem Timeline Evidence
tasks.description: Separate observed filesystem values from inference and attribution.
tasks.problemStatement: Given synthetic ext4 metadata, classify each statement as observation, inference, or unsupported attribution.
tasks.hint: Do not rename ctime as creation time.
tasks.solutionCode: Observation: filesystem reports ctime T. Inference: inode state changed near T. Unsupported: a named person intentionally performed the change.

modules.title: journald, Audit, Authentication, and Retention
modules.description: Analyze Linux logs, audit telemetry, authentication, privilege use, and evidence gaps.

lessons.title: systemd-journald
lessons.description: Query bounded journal records and interpret retention correctly.

notes.text: systemd-journald collects structured records from multiple sources. journalctl can filter by time, unit, and priority.

items: Journal persistence and retention depend on configuration.
A query reports what matching records remain available.

practicals.title: Bounded Journal Review
practicals.description: Run read-only journal queries and document source, time, and limitations.
steps: Record gaps without modifying the journal.
practicals.solution:
```bash
journalctl --list-boots
journalctl --since "1 hour ago" --until "now"
journalctl -u systemd-logind.service --since "1 hour ago" --until "now"
```
practicals.output: The exact records depend on the lab host. No fixed log output should be expected.

quiz.question: What does a bounded journalctl query establish?
options: What matching records are present in the selected journal/time range
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: What matching records are present in the selected journal/time range
quiz.explanation: The query is bounded by source, time, filters, and retention.

summary: Journal evidence must be interpreted with configuration and retention context.

lessons.title: Linux Audit and ausearch
lessons.description: Understand auditd and query audit records while checking configuration assumptions.

notes.text: auditd writes audit records; ausearch and aureport inspect them. Recorded coverage depends on audit configuration and rules.

items: Audit is configurable telemetry.
Historical rule configuration may be essential to explain missing records.

quiz.question: What most directly affects Linux Audit coverage?
options: It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: The audit rules/configuration in effect
quiz.explanation: Enabled rules determine which audit events are generated.

summary: Audit evidence is powerful but not universal.

lessons.title: Authentication and Privilege Evidence
lessons.description: Correlate SSH/PAM, sudo, audit, and journal records while separating account identity from human attribution.

notes.text: A successful authentication record establishes a system-observed authentication event for an account or mechanism. It does not independently identify the physical operator.

items: Shared accounts and stolen credentials complicate attribution.
Post-login activity should be correlated with process and filesystem evidence.

quiz.question: What is the safest conclusion from a successful SSH login record?
options: The system recorded successful authentication for the account
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: The system recorded successful authentication for the account
quiz.explanation: The record supports the authentication event; attribution and subsequent activity need additional evidence.

summary: Account identity and human identity are different evidence questions.

lessons.title: Rotation, Retention, and Centralized Logs
lessons.description: Investigate missing log periods without assuming deliberate deletion.

notes.text: Logs can rotate, compress, expire, or be centrally forwarded. Missing data can also result from clock errors, acquisition scope, storage issues, or deliberate deletion.

items: Retention is part of evidence completeness.
Never fill a gap with an invented event.

quiz.question: What should an examiner do when an expected log period is missing?
options: Check retention, rotation, configuration, time sources, remote logging, and scope
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: Check retention, rotation, configuration, time sources, remote logging, and scope
quiz.explanation: Multiple benign and technical explanations must be tested before concluding deliberate manipulation.

summary: Evidence gaps should be documented and investigated.

tasks.title: Correlate Login-to-Privilege Activity
tasks.description: Create a source-preserving sequence from synthetic auth, sudo, and audit data.
tasks.problemStatement: Correlate a successful SSH event, sudo authorization, and command event.
tasks.hint: Do not translate account names into people.
tasks.solutionCode: Conclusion: the host recorded authentication followed by privileged command activity; physical operator identity remains unresolved.
tasks.solutionExplanation: Cross-source correlation increases confidence without inventing attribution.

modules.title: Processes, /proc, Shells, and Persistence
modules.description: Investigate live process state, shell history, systemd units, timers, and cron without changing evidence.

lessons.title: /proc Live-State Triage
lessons.description: Use /proc for controlled point-in-time process inspection.

notes.text: proc is a virtual filesystem exposing kernel and process information. Entries such as /proc/PID/status and /proc/PID/cmdline represent live state.

items: PIDs can disappear during collection.
/proc is not a historical database.

practicals.title: Process Snapshot
practicals.description: Collect selected /proc evidence for a benign process.
practicals.solution:
```bash
PID=$(pgrep -n systemd || true)
if [ -n "$PID" ]; then cat /proc/$PID/status; tr "\0" " " < /proc/$PID/cmdline; echo; ls -l /proc/$PID/fd; fi
```
practicals.output: Output varies by host. The important result is recognizing live-state volatility.

quiz.question: What is the main limitation of /proc evidence?
options: It reflects live state and is time-sensitive
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: It reflects live state and is time-sensitive
quiz.explanation: proc is a live kernel interface.

summary: Live triage requires timestamps and collection notes.

lessons.title: Shell History
lessons.description: Interpret shell history as contextual evidence rather than a complete execution log.

notes.text: Shell history behavior depends on shell configuration and use. Commands can be omitted, altered, disabled, or executed outside interactive shells.

items: Audit/process telemetry can corroborate execution.
Never inject test commands into real case data.

quiz.question: Why is shell history incomplete?
options: It can be absent/altered and misses other execution paths
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: It can be absent/altered and misses other execution paths
quiz.explanation: History is user-space evidence with coverage limitations.

summary: Use shell history with independent sources.

lessons.title: systemd Services and Timers
lessons.description: Inspect current service/timer configuration and correlate it with execution telemetry.

notes.text: An enabled systemd unit establishes current configuration state. It does not, alone, prove when it was created or that it executed.

items: Journal/audit/process records can establish execution.
Forensic inspection should be read-only.

quiz.question: What does an enabled systemd unit establish by itself?
options: It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: Current enabled configuration
quiz.explanation: Configuration and observed execution are distinct evidence classes.

summary: Persistence analysis combines configuration and execution evidence.

lessons.title: Cron and Scheduled Execution
lessons.description: Interpret cron definitions and distinguish configured schedules from observed execution.

notes.text: Cron entries describe scheduled commands. They do not automatically prove that a scheduled command ran successfully.

items: Correlate cron definitions with logs and audit events.
Do not modify schedules during examination.

quiz.question: What does a cron entry directly show?
options: It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: A scheduled command is configured
quiz.explanation: A cron entry is configuration evidence, not execution proof.

summary: Scheduled execution requires corroborating telemetry.

tasks.title: Reconstruct an Execution Chain
tasks.description: Correlate service, process, shell, and audit evidence.
tasks.problemStatement: Determine whether a scheduled-service process chain is internally consistent and identify missing evidence.
tasks.hint: Start from parent-child relationships, then validate timing and source semantics.
tasks.solutionCode: Supported: a service-related execution chain exists in the synthetic records. Unproven: authorship and malicious intent.

modules.title: Users, Permissions, Capabilities, and Links
modules.description: Interpret Linux identity, access configuration, capabilities, extended attributes, and link semantics.

lessons.title: UID/GID and Account State
lessons.description: Interpret Linux account mappings and session evidence.
learningObjectives: separate configured accounts from observed use

notes.text: UIDs and GIDs are numeric identities used by Linux permissions and process credentials. NSS may provide identity information beyond local files.

items: Configured account state is not proof of interactive use.
Do not expose password hashes or secrets.

quiz.question: What does a UID provide?
options: A numeric OS identity used for ownership and process credentials
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: A numeric OS identity used for ownership and process credentials
quiz.explanation: UID is a numeric identity used by Linux access-control mechanisms.

summary: Identity mapping is not human attribution.

lessons.title: Permissions and ACLs
lessons.description: Read mode bits and ACLs as access configuration.
learningObjectives: separate allowed access from observed access

notes.text: Mode bits express owner/group/other permissions. POSIX ACLs can add entries beyond basic mode bits when supported.

items: Permissions describe authorization state.
Actual access needs access-event evidence.

practicals.title: Permission and ACL Inspection
practicals.description: Create controlled lab files and inspect their permissions.
practicals.solution:
```bash
mkdir -p lab-perms
printf A > lab-perms/a
printf B > lab-perms/b
chmod 600 lab-perms/a
chmod 644 lab-perms/b
stat -c "%A %U %G %a %n" lab-perms/a lab-perms/b
getfacl lab-perms/a 2>/dev/null || true
```
practicals.output: The output shows access configuration; it does not prove a user actually accessed the files.

quiz.question: What does mode 600 mean under basic permissions?
options: Owner read/write; group and others none
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: Owner read/write; group and others none
quiz.explanation: 600 grants read/write to owner and no permissions to group or others.

summary: Access configuration is not access history.

lessons.title: Linux Capabilities
lessons.description: Analyze fine-grained privileges as configuration/state.

notes.text: Linux capabilities divide selected privileged operations into units. They may be associated with processes or file metadata.

items: A capability indicates privilege, not intent.
Do not modify capabilities on evidence.

quiz.question: What is a Linux capability?
options: It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: A distinct unit of privilege
quiz.explanation: Capabilities represent fine-grained privileged operations.

summary: Privilege evidence needs execution and usage context.

lessons.title: Extended Attributes and Links
lessons.description: Interpret xattrs, symlinks, and hard links and their collection implications.

notes.text: Extended attributes attach name/value metadata. A symlink stores a path reference; a hard link is another directory entry to the same inode.

items: Following symlinks can cross an evidence-root boundary.
Link semantics can affect file identity and duplication analysis.

quiz.question: Why can symlinks matter during forensic collection?
options: They can point outside the intended evidence tree
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: They can point outside the intended evidence tree
quiz.explanation: A path-based collector can accidentally leave the intended root by following symlink targets.

summary: Safe traversal is a forensic boundary control.

tasks.title: Assess a Privilege-Capability Finding
tasks.description: Evaluate whether a capability finding warrants escalation.
tasks.problemStatement: Separate evidence that a capability exists from evidence that a binary executed or used the privilege.
tasks.hint: Analyze the inference chain one step at a time.
tasks.solutionCode: The capability establishes privileged configuration. It does not by itself establish execution, misuse, or authorship.

modules.title: Network, SSH, Packages, and Application Data
modules.description: Correlate live network state, SSH configuration/authentication, package provenance, and SQLite application evidence.

lessons.title: Socket and Network State
lessons.description: Use live socket and interface state as point-in-time evidence.

notes.text: ss reports socket state; interface and route commands describe configuration at collection time. Historical activity requires retained telemetry.

items: An IP address is not a human identity.
Encrypted traffic may still expose metadata without plaintext.

quiz.question: What is the main limitation of ss forensics?
options: It is primarily a point-in-time view of socket state
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: It is primarily a point-in-time view of socket state
quiz.explanation: The command provides current socket state unless persistent telemetry is also available.

summary: Network evidence gains value through correlation.

lessons.title: SSH Evidence
lessons.description: Correlate SSH configuration and authentication events.
learningObjectives: separate allowed access from observed use

notes.text: SSH configuration can define authentication methods and access settings. Authorized keys show configured access; authentication logs show observed events.

items: Post-login process and sudo evidence can establish subsequent activity.
Never copy private keys or tokens into reports.

practicals.title: SSH Correlation Lab
practicals.description: Inspect controlled SSH configuration and correlate it with journal records.
steps: Query a bounded SSH-related log period.
Compare key configuration with recorded authentication.
State one supported conclusion and one limitation.
practicals.solution:
```bash
sshd -T 2>/dev/null | grep -E "^(port|passwordauthentication|pubkeyauthentication)$" || true
journalctl --since "24 hours ago" | grep -Ei "sshd|ssh" | tail -100
```
practicals.output: Exact records vary by lab host. The result should keep configuration and observed authentication separate.

quiz.question: What does an authorized SSH public key primarily establish?
options: The account is configured to permit that key
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: The account is configured to permit that key
quiz.explanation: Configuration establishes permitted authentication state, not observed use.

summary: SSH findings should combine configuration and event records.

lessons.title: Package Provenance
lessons.description: Use package databases to contextualize binaries.

notes.text: Package systems can map installed paths to package ownership on supported distributions. A file outside package ownership may be locally compiled or copied.

items: Package ownership does not identify the person who installed software.
Do not alter package state during examination.

quiz.question: What can package ownership tell an examiner?
options: A path is associated with an installed package
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: A path is associated with an installed package
quiz.explanation: It supplies provenance/context about installed software.

summary: Package context is useful but not a complete attribution mechanism.

lessons.title: SQLite Application Evidence
lessons.description: Inspect a SQLite artifact read-only and preserve schema/timestamp semantics.

notes.text: Applications may use SQLite to store history and state. Schema and timestamp semantics are application-specific.

items: Read-only access reduces accidental modification.
A syntactically correct query can still support a wrong interpretation if schema is misunderstood.

quiz.question: Why inspect the SQLite schema first?
options: To understand data structure and avoid incorrect assumptions
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: To understand data structure and avoid incorrect assumptions
quiz.explanation: The schema defines tables/fields and their relationships.

summary: Application data requires schema-aware interpretation.

tasks.title: Correlate Remote-Access Evidence
tasks.description: Build a source-preserving SSH activity sequence.
tasks.problemStatement: Combine configured access, authentication, process, and network observations.
tasks.hint: Keep account identity separate from human identity.
tasks.solutionCode: The records can support a sequence of configured access→authentication→process activity, while human attribution remains unresolved.

modules.title: Memory Forensics with Volatility 3
modules.description: Use current Volatility 3 Linux plugins on permitted memory images and understand acquisition limitations.

lessons.title: Volatile Memory Fundamentals
lessons.description: Understand what RAM can answer and why acquisition is disruptive.

notes.text: RAM can contain processes, command lines, mappings, sockets, modules, and transient secrets/tokens in some contexts. A memory image is a snapshot.

items: Acquisition can change memory.
Volatility 3 analyzes memory images; it is not a general Linux memory-acquisition tool.

quiz.question: What is a defining memory-image limitation?
options: It represents volatile state at a particular time
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: It represents volatile state at a particular time
quiz.explanation: Memory is dynamic and the image captures only a point-in-time state.

summary: Memory analysis complements persistent evidence.

lessons.title: Volatility 3 Linux Process Analysis
lessons.description: Run current Linux process plugins and interpret ancestry.

notes.text: Current Volatility 3 documentation includes Linux process plugins such as `linux.pslist`, `linux.pstree`, and `linux.psaux`. Linux symbol information may be required.

items: Output varies with image and symbols.
Use permitted training memory images only.

practicals.title: Analyze a Training Memory Image
practicals.description: Run process plugins against an instructor-provided or permitted public training image.
steps: Select one lead and state one benign alternative explanation.
practicals.solution:
```bash
python3 vol.py -f linux-memdump.raw linux.pslist > pslist.txt
python3 vol.py -f linux-memdump.raw linux.pstree > pstree.txt
python3 vol.py -f linux-memdump.raw linux.psaux > psaux.txt
```
practicals.output: Exact process output depends on the memory image. The important result is correct procedure and cautious interpretation.

quiz.question: What does linux.pstree primarily provide?
options: It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: Process parent/child relationships
quiz.explanation: The plugin adds execution context through process ancestry.

summary: Current plugin documentation should guide use.

lessons.title: Memory Anomalies and Corroboration
lessons.description: Use loaded modules and process anomalies as leads requiring disk/log validation.

notes.text: An unusual module or process chain is a lead. Validate path, file bytes, package ownership, persistence, and logs when available.

items: Unfamiliar is not synonymous with malicious.
Persistent evidence can validate volatile findings.

quiz.question: Why correlate a suspicious memory module with disk evidence?
options: To validate path, bytes, provenance, and persistence
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: To validate path, bytes, provenance, and persistence
quiz.explanation: Persistent evidence provides context missing from a volatile snapshot.

summary: Memory creates leads; corroboration supports conclusions.

tasks.title: Triage a Linux Memory Anomaly
tasks.description: Evaluate a synthetic Volatility process/module finding.
tasks.problemStatement: Decide whether escalation is justified and specify the evidence needed before calling it malicious.
tasks.hint: Separate anomaly detection from malware classification.
tasks.solutionCode: Escalate for deeper validation, then correlate module path/hash, package ownership, persistence, and logs.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task models disciplined memory triage.

modules.title: Timelines, Anti-Forensics, Validation, Reporting, and Project
modules.description: Construct defensible timelines, recognize evidence gaps, validate tools, report findings, and complete the final project.

lessons.title: Source-Preserving Timelines
lessons.description: Build timelines that retain original timestamps and artifact provenance.

notes.text: A timeline is a derived analytical dataset. Keep source timestamp and artifact alongside any normalized value.

items: Do not silently resolve contradictions.
Each important event should be traceable back to evidence.

practicals.title: Build a Linux Timeline
practicals.description: Merge synthetic journal, audit, and filesystem CSV files.
practicals.solution:
```python
import csv
sources={"journal.csv":"journal","audit.csv":"audit","filesystem.csv":"filesystem"}
events=[]
for fn,src in sources.items():
    with open(fn,newline="",encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for r in csv.DictReader(f): events.append({"source":src,"source_time":r["timestamp"],"event":r["event"]})
events.sort(key=lambda e:e["source_time"])
with open("timeline.csv","w",newline="",encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w=csv.DictWriter(f,fieldnames=["source","source_time","event"]); w.writeheader(); w.writerows(events)
```
practicals.output: The output is a chronological analytical view with source provenance.

quiz.question: What makes a derived timeline traceable?
options: Each event links to a source artifact and preserves time semantics
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: Each event links to a source artifact and preserves time semantics
quiz.explanation: Traceability connects derived rows to the evidence from which they were produced.

summary: Timeline construction is analysis, not original evidence.

lessons.title: Anti-Forensics Awareness
lessons.description: Recognize wiping, log clearing, timestamp manipulation, and encryption as evidence-gap categories.

notes.text: Evidence loss can result from wiping or clearing, but also from retention, configuration, clock problems, acquisition limits, or normal system behavior.

items: Treat evidence gaps as hypotheses to investigate.
Do not perform destructive evasion techniques in labs unless explicitly authorized and safe.

quiz.question: What should happen when an expected artifact is missing?
options: Test retention, configuration, clock, acquisition, and scope before concluding manipulation
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: Test retention, configuration, clock, acquisition, and scope before concluding manipulation
quiz.explanation: Multiple explanations must be considered before concluding deliberate evidence destruction.

summary: The course focuses on defensive recognition, not evasion procedures.

lessons.title: Tool Validation
lessons.description: Validate forensic functions using known data and preserved tool context.

notes.text: Tool validation is function- and condition-specific. A known test image with expected artifacts provides a stronger basis than popularity or recency alone.

items: Record tool version, environment, configuration, and expected results.
Preserve scripts and derived outputs where reproducibility matters.

quiz.question: Which is a strong tool-validation test?
options: Run a known test image with expected artifacts and compare results
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: Run a known test image with expected artifacts and compare results
quiz.explanation: Controlled expected data allows a defined forensic function to be tested.

summary: Validation supports repeatability and review.

lessons.title: Forensic Reporting
lessons.description: Write findings using observation, corroboration, interpretation, and limitation.

notes.text: A useful report contains scope, evidence, integrity, methods, tools/versions, findings, limitations, conclusions, and supporting exhibits.

items: Use the narrowest claim supported by evidence.
Do not convert account activity into human identity without additional evidence.

quiz.question: Which report wording is strongest when attribution is uncertain?
options: The system recorded successful authentication for account X at 18:42Z
It is unrelated to the lesson
quiz.answer: The system recorded successful authentication for account X at 18:42Z
quiz.explanation: The first statement is directly tied to a system record and avoids unsupported attribution.

summary: Strong reports expose limitations.

lessons.title: Case Closure and Reproducibility
lessons.description: Prepare evidence, methods, derived outputs, and reports for future review.

notes.text: Closure can include evidence hashes, custody/provenance, working-copy derivation, tool versions, scripts, queries, reports, exhibits, and archive controls.

items: Do not store passwords, tokens, or private keys in ordinary reports.
Retention and access controls should follow the case environment.

project.name: Linux Forensic Evidence Triage Workbench
project.description: A read-only Python workbench for an authorized Linux evidence working directory. It inventories regular files, computes SHA-256, records generic filesystem times available through Python, detects duplicate content, and writes structured reports outside the evidence root.
steps: Create synthetic nested evidence with a zero-byte file and a duplicate-content pair.
Create the project files from the embedded code.
Verify file count, hashes, timestamps, and duplicate groups.
Modify only a working copy and observe the changed digest.
Attempt an output directory inside the evidence root and verify refusal.

code.main.py:
from __future__ import annotations
import argparse,sys
from pathlib import Path
from forensic_core import collect_records,write_csv,write_json,write_duplicates

ap=argparse.ArgumentParser(description='Read-only Linux forensic triage')
ap.add_argument('evidence_dir',type=Path)
ap.add_argument('--output',type=Path,default=Path('forensic_report'))
a=ap.parse_args()
root=a.evidence_dir.resolve(); out=a.output.resolve()
if not root.is_dir(): print('Evidence directory does not exist',file=sys.stderr); raise SystemExit(2)
if out==root or root in out.parents: print('Refusing to write reports inside evidence directory',file=sys.stderr); raise SystemExit(2)
out.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
records=collect_records(root)
write_csv(records,out/'file_inventory.csv'); write_json(records,out/'file_inventory.json'); write_duplicates(records,out/'duplicate_groups.json')
print(f'Files examined: {len(records)}')
code.README.md: Educational, read-only triage project. Analyze only authorized working copies or evidence exports; this does not replace validated acquisition or forensic suites.

project.explanation: The project separates evidence input from generated reports, hashes regular files in chunks, records generic filesystem timestamps as derived metadata, excludes symlinks from regular-file traversal, groups identical content by SHA-256, and includes unit tests. It deliberately does not acquire disk images, recover deleted data, parse filesystem-native journals, or acquire RAM. Those functions require specialist tools and validated procedures.
validationPlan: Test nested files and duplicate contents.
Modify only a working copy and confirm the digest changes.
Verify unsafe output paths are rejected.
Review that evidence files are only opened for reading.
limitations: Python stat fields are not a replacement for native forensic filesystem parsing.
The utility does not establish authorship or intent.
Hash equality establishes content equality, not provenance.
Actual investigations require appropriate authorization and evidentiary procedures.
